questions.q: What real-world problem did NAT solve that made it necessary long before IPv6 saw wide adoption?
options: IPv4 address exhaustion — not enough public addresses for every device on Earth
Slow Wi-Fi speeds in large offices
DNS servers running out of names to assign
MAC address collisions between vendors
questions.explain: IPv4 only has about 4.3 billion addresses, nowhere near enough for every device, so NAT let entire private networks share a small number of public addresses.

questions.q: In NAT/PAT, how does a router keep track of which internal device a reply belongs to when many devices share one public IP?
options: It broadcasts the reply to every internal device
It uses a NAT table mapping each internal device's connection to a specific public port, and rewrites addresses using that table
It assigns a new public IP to each device automatically
It drops all replies and requires manual port forwarding for everything
questions.explain: PAT distinguishes connections by port number — the router's NAT table maps each internal address:port pair to a unique public port, and rewrites addresses in both directions using that mapping.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a stateful and a stateless firewall?
options: A stateless firewall is always faster with no real tradeoff
A stateful firewall tracks active connections and automatically allows the matching reply; a stateless firewall evaluates every packet in isolation with no memory of prior traffic
A stateful firewall can only block UDP traffic
There is no real difference between the two
questions.explain: Stateful firewalls remember which outbound requests were approved and auto-permit their replies; stateless firewalls need an explicit rule for both directions since they have no memory of prior packets.

questions.q: What fields does a basic ACL/firewall rule typically evaluate on each packet?
options: Only the packet's physical cable length
Source, destination, protocol, port, and the action (permit or deny)
Only the destination MAC address
Only whether the packet is encrypted
questions.explain: A typical ACL rule checks source, destination, protocol (TCP/UDP/ICMP/etc.), port, and then applies its action — permit or deny.

questions.q: When a packet is checked against an ordered list of ACL rules, what determines which rule actually applies?
options: The last rule in the list always wins
All matching rules apply simultaneously
The first rule that matches wins — rules are evaluated top to bottom and evaluation stops at the first match
The shortest rule in the list always wins
questions.explain: ACLs are evaluated top to bottom, and the first matching rule's action is applied; no further rules are checked after that match.
